title: The Foolish Heart
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: The Nature of the Fool
subpoints: Distinction between the 'simple' (ignorant) and the 'fool' (willful denial)
The fool lives as if God does not exist to suppress conscience
Foolishness is a corruption of God's original design

outline.title: The Universal Condition of Humanity
subpoints: All humanity apart from Christ is described as 'fools'
No one does moral good without trusting in God
Righteousness apart from God is like filthy rags

outline.title: God’s Search for the Righteous
subpoints: God perpetually looks down from heaven to seek those who understand and seek Him
The 'looking down' motif often precedes judgment (Flood, Babel, Sodom)
God desires people who understand His law and pursue Him with thirst

summary:
In this sermon, Pastor Tito Lyro examines Psalm 14, focusing on the biblical definition of the 'fool' as one who willfully denies the existence of God despite having knowledge of Him. The message distinguishes between the 'simple,' who are ignorant and in need of instruction, and the 'fool,' who has been instructed but chooses to live in rebellion against that truth. This willful denial is described as a corruption of the human design, resulting in a life devoid of true moral goodness, as the supreme good is defined by trust in God.

The sermon further explores the universal scope of this condition, asserting that all humanity apart from Christ falls under the description of the fool. By referencing Romans 1, it is explained that while God’s invisible attributes are clearly seen in creation, people suppress the truth in unrighteousness, leading to darkened hearts. Consequently, even the best human acts are tainted by sin and insufficient without reliance on God.

Finally, the text highlights God’s perpetual search for those who understand His law and seek Him. The imagery of God 'looking down from heaven' is contextualized with other biblical instances such as the Flood and the Tower of Babel, indicating that this divine observation often precedes judgment. The sermon concludes by emphasizing God’s desire for a people who, like the psalmist in Psalm 63, thirst for Him and pursue a relationship with the Creator.
